label: Institution
name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
summary:
The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Fort Wayne, Indiana, USA (completed 1859, current cathedral since 1857), is the mother church of the Diocese of Fort Wayne-South Bend — one of the oldest Catholic dioceses in the American Midwest, covering Notre Dame University's home territory. Built in the Gothic Revival style by architect Patrick Charles Keely (who designed over 700 Catholic churches in America), the cathedral represents the frontier Catholicism of mid-19th-century Midwestern settlement, serving the German and Irish immigrant communities that built Fort Wayne's industrial base.

Keely's cathedral design (1857-1859) used the Gothic Revival aesthetic then fashionable for Catholic American churches — pointed arches, stone facade, and stained glass windows — scaled to a frontier city that had only 2,000 residents at its founding. Fort Wayne's Catholicism was shaped by the University of Notre Dame (30 miles south) and the Congregation of Holy Cross — the priests who founded Notre Dame in 1842 also served early Fort Wayne's Catholic community.

The Cathedral Basilica designation (granted by Pope Francis in 2019) elevated it to minor basilica status — one of approximately 85 minor basilicas in the United States. The current cathedral serves as the spiritual center for Indiana's second-largest Catholic diocese, encompassing 14 counties across northern Indiana. Its connection to Notre Dame University — America's most famous Catholic university — makes it theologically and institutionally significant within American Catholicism.
